Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a short announcement for a new feature in a note-taking app: offline sync. Around 200 words.

Offline sync is now available in version 3.2.

Until now, editing a note without a connection meant the app queued your changes locally and pushed them the next time it reached the server. If you edited the same note on your phone and laptop while both were offline, whichever device reconnected second overwrote the first. People lost work that way, and we heard about it.

The new sync engine tracks changes per paragraph instead of per note. When two offline copies of a note come back online, the app merges paragraphs that were edited separately and flags only the ones where both devices changed the same text. You resolve those in a side-by-side view that shows each version with its device name and timestamp.

Offline edits now sync in under two seconds on reconnect for notebooks up to 5,000 notes. Above that, expect a first sync of ten to thirty seconds while the app rebuilds its index, then the same two-second behaviour after.

Attachments still require a connection to upload. An image added offline stays on the device and uploads when you reconnect, with a marker in the note showing it is pending.

Offline sync is on by default. To turn it off, go to Settings, then Sync, and switch off "Work offline".

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Add a paragraph about what happens when two devices edit the same note offline.

When two devices edit the same note offline, neither one wins by default. The app keeps both versions and compares them paragraph by paragraph. Paragraphs that only one device touched merge in without a prompt, so a note edited at the top on your laptop and at the bottom on your phone comes back whole. Where both devices changed the same paragraph, the note opens with those sections marked and a side-by-side view showing each version, the device that wrote it, and the time. You pick one, or edit a third version in place. Nothing overwrites until you choose, and the unresolved copy stays in the note's history for thirty days if you change your mind.
